en: He spoke of heart-rending sorrow:
‘Your father's grave, forty warriors!
When shall we honor the ancestral spirit?
Manas, whose spirit is sacred—
How can we piss upon his salt?
Attacking his child,
What desire shall we fulfill?
We forty were dogs come from forty places;
We shall go back to chasing pigs.
Manas, whose spirit is sacred—
Does not his spirit stand here now?
Will not his spirit strike us down?
The blessed, gray-maned Manas's
Only son, Semetey—
Can good come of attacking him?
Your father's grave, forty warriors!
Manas, who went to the other world—
Can we let his spirit strike us down?
When the hero Manas lived,
Consider it, forty warriors,
We used to swagger grandly.
An entire otter pelt
We would split in half,
And put upon our trouser legs.
Now, let alone otter, there is no lambskin.
Is this the hour of your ruin?
Your father's grave, forty warriors!
Like puppies left at an abandoned camp,
Now is the hour of your howling.
Before, when Manas lived,
When bored, we hunted roe deer;
When not bored, in Talas
We played freely at our ease.
When leopard Manas lived,
When the Bloodthirsty One was safe,
Your father's grave, forty warriors!
You went and took the Afghan land;
How could Margilan remain unharmed?
When that Manas lived,
We plundered, destroyed and took the craftswomen.
With thimble mouths and camel-calf eyes,
From the beauties who swayed as they walked,
We chose and took the girls.
We wore five apiece in a day.
To Beijing, beyond the reach of the Flood,
We brought uproar and attacked.
We fought our enemies together,
We pursued our claims together.
When mighty Manas lived,
We broke through the middle and made a road.
We destroyed Omsk and took spoils.
Since that Manas passed away,
Let alone spoils, we cannot find plain cotton cloth.
Where have we become mighty?
We have been humiliated by six villains.
One warrior came from the Russians,
One warrior came from the Chinese,
One warrior came from Crimea.
We forty were dogs come from forty places;
What people were we, if not dogs?
When we came to this Manas,
One warrior came without a horse.
To the warrior who came without a horse,
With argali feet and copper forelegs,
He gave a true peerless steed to ride.
One warrior came without a coat.
To the warrior who came without a coat,
He clothed him in the finest coat.
One warrior came without a home.
The warrior who came without a home,
With golden roof ring and copper binding band,
He housed in a great royal dwelling.
One warrior came without a wife.
For the warrior who came without a wife,
In crimson dresses, with slender waists,
Graceful, with camel-calf eyes,
He gathered the most beautiful girls.
The mullahs and the khojas
He had perform a hurried marriage rite.
The hero Manas obtained wives for them.
One warrior came without livestock.
To the warrior who came without livestock,
White-marked horses upon the hills,
Thoroughbreds and noble steeds together,
Khan Manas gave his animals.
Your father's grave, forty warriors!
When Manas, favored by Khizr, died,
It seems we all died too.
With the hair upon our napes bristling,
We have become beasts.
Rushing wherever someone cries, “There!”
We have become hunting dogs.
By raising Abyke and Kobosh
As khans, our desire
We seem to have fulfilled!
At Manas, who went to the other world,
We fire upon his spirit.
Turning into beasts,
From the very form of humanity,
We have departed.
Manas, whose salt lays a heavy bond—
How can we piss upon his salt?
Against Manas's goshawk son,
With what face can we raise a hand?
I leave you to God, forty pigs!
Where is the writing knotted in your belts?
Embracing and becoming friends,
Where is the oath sworn before God?
The hero Manas, the gray-maned one's
Only child, Semetey—
How can we go in shooting?
Forty pigs who do not fear God,
How can we attack the child?
Fighting with a child,
What desire shall we fulfill?
If what is said is true,
We shall turn into black donkeys.
Against Manas's only son,
Can anyone who raises a hand prosper?
Goshawk Manas, the gray-maned one's
Salt—one who means it harm,
Can he be a true Muslim?
I will have none of these words of yours.
Against Manas's only son,
Even if my head is cut off, I will not raise a hand.
I shall not perish fighting him.
The gray-maned hero who went to the other world—
I shall not estrange myself from his spirit.
Against the orphan who has now arrived,
I shall not go to face him in battle.
I will have none of these words of yours.
Noble-steeded Manas, the gray-maned one's
Only son, I shall not attack.
Your origin was among the kites.
Since dear Manas died,
You have all become a motley band.
When gray-maned Manas lived,
We pursued our enemies.
Since Abyke and Kobosh came,
Let alone enemies, finding no claim to pursue,
All our elders have been troubled.
Your father's grave, forty warriors!
Since magnanimous Manas died,
We have all become fools!
The renowned Khan Manas died,
And all forty warriors died with him.
Your father's grave, forty warriors!
We forty were people come from forty places.
Not one would heed another,
Not one could bear to see another;
We were a snarling pack of dogs.
We were a motley gathering, not a people.
Your leaders Abyke and Kobosh could take no wolf;
Noble Manas, who did take wolves,
Those villains cannot bear to see.
When the hero Manas lived,
Eating yearlings still suckling their barren dams,
Eating horse rump with a span of fat,
Drunk on spirits and panting,
Eager to spring at every foe,
Heated with kumis,
Our bones and skin growing hot,
Did you not pass your days so, forty warriors,
Making a clamor in broad Talas?
Forty warriors full of insolence,
Upon magnanimous Sultan Manas's
Only son we raise our hands;
Now we have become forty pigs.
Semetey, against whom you wage a holy war,
Is the spring feeding the river,
Sultan Manas, the leopard's
Lamp gained through mortal suffering.
For you to sweep down in holy war,
To stand trading mighty blows,
He is no mountain dark with haze,
Nor an enemy come from the Kalmyks.
He is no mountain red with haze,
For you to shout and wage a holy war,
Nor an enemy come from China.
Before the unswerving ancestral spirit,
The forty pig-warriors will not go unscathed.’
Speaking thus, the hero Yrchy Uul
Mourned the former days.
His heart burned with grief,
And the servant Shuutu halted with him.
The rest of the forty warriors
Abused the two of them.
‘Manas's only orphan
You have taken as your protector!
The fugitive woman Kanykei
You have taken as your support!
Manas's son will bring no good;
He will leave none of us unharmed.
Yrchy and Shuutu the servant,
We shall seize you two first,
And slaughter you as a sacrifice.
Then on the orphan son of Manas,
We shall take our vengeance!’
When they spoke like this,
Shuutu stood and said:
‘Upon the orphan son of Manas,
Your father's grave, forty warriors,
You have advanced straight with spears extended.
Before those who see and hear,
You have brought utter disgrace!
Shame! Shame upon your faces!
Your father's grave, forty pigs!
May foxes sniff at your flesh!
Who now would look upon your faces?’
Yrchy Uul and Shuutu the servant,
Their countless treasures and possessions,
The two scattered and left behind.
Without attacking Semetey,
Each turning toward his own land,
The two fled away.
When dawn broke clear and white,
When light fell upon the earth,
When the Taraza star set from the sky,
When dawn rose in fullness,
And the light of dawn spread apart,
And light appeared upon the earth,
At just such a time,
Mottled blue flags appeared.
The army clamored and divided,
People of many kinds swept forward,
The troops surged on without breaking ranks.
Roaring in their wrath,
Shouting ‘Kobosh!’ as their battle cry,
Raging like rabid dogs,
The forty warriors came in a frenzy.
Abyke and his men raised a clamor;
Earth flew up and dust blazed.
They swarmed in a mass.
God, do not let us see their faces!
Like flying tumbleweed,
They charged and began the battle,
Laid a fierce siege,
And brought devastation.
With shrill cries and clamor,
With a roaring, massed assault,
The trumpets boomed,
The war drums rattled.
With shrill cries and clamor,
They drew bows in a rain of arrows,
And fired bullets like hail.
Khan Manas's forty warriors
Girded their waists firmly,
And attacked like monsters.
All stood against them,
Fighting without sparing their lives.
At Chachykei's fortress,
At Kanykei's royal court,
Khan Manas's forty warriors
Formed a circle,
And enclosed it in their midst.
